This is more than unusual because there is no corresponding memory or appraisal content linking police violence to ex-partner or childbirth themes.

This coping item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly anchored compared with the other selected strategies.

vignette:
Elena Martinez was seventy-nine years old, a widow for thirteen years, and a former combat pilot who had flown helicopter gunships in Vietnam. The memory of that war had never troubled her the way the afternoon at the Oakwood Market did. She had stopped there on a humid Tuesday in June two years ago, picking up vegetables and a bag of limes. The market was crowded—voices overlapping, carts bumping hips—and she remembered feeling impatient, eager to get home. Then she heard the sirens. They grew louder, stopped directly outside. Two officers entered, scanning the produce aisles. One of them pointed at her. She did not understand why. They asked for identification, and when she reached slowly for her wallet, the second officer grabbed her arm, twisted it behind her back, and slammed her face into a stack of melons. She smelled the rind bursting, felt the grit of concrete on her cheek, heard the crack of her own shoulder socket dislocating. She was handcuffed, shouting that she was a veteran, that she had done nothing. They held her on the ground for seventeen minutes before a supervisor arrived and released her. There was no apology. The charges were never filed; the paperwork was lost.

For the first few weeks Elena could not sleep. She stayed up until two or three in the morning, sitting in the dark of her living room, watching the street through the blinds. She told herself it was to avoid the nightmares, but what really happened was that when she closed her eyes the memory came back not as a story but as pieces—the wet smell of melon, the blinding pressure of the floor against her temple, the sound of her own breath trapped beneath a body. She could not predict when a piece would arrive. She would be chopping onions and suddenly see the officer’s badge, the metal glint inches from her face, and then it was gone. She began to avoid crowds. The market where it happened had been crowded, and now any place with more than a few bodies felt like a trap. She stopped going to the grocery store; her daughter delivered food once a week. She stopped attending the veterans’ community center, where she used to play dominos with the other retirees.

Elena also stopped wearing the olive-green jacket she had worn that day. She had bought it at a thrift store and liked the weight of it, but now any jacket with a similar cut made her stomach knot. She threw the original away but began to notice that other people’s jackets—parkas, windbreakers, even a child’s fleece in the same shade—made her shoulders stiffen. She started scanning every room she entered: for weapons, for objects that could be used as weapons, for the silhouette of a utility belt. At the bus stop she would catalogue the knives visible in open kitchens, the hammer in a neighbor’s tool belt, the baseball bat leaning against a garage wall. Her daughter once asked why she kept looking behind them as they walked. Elena said she was checking for threats. Her daughter said, “Mom, you’re in San Diego. It’s safe.” Elena did not argue, but she knew that safety was a feeling she no longer had access to. Even in her own bedroom, with the door locked and the windows sealed, her heart would pound at the distant wail of a siren. She would freeze, unable to relax until the sound faded and she had verified that no police car was on her street.

The physical reactions were the worst part. A car backfiring, a loud voice in a hallway—her body would react before her mind caught up: sweating, trembling, a rush of heat that made her dizzy. She had always been physically tough, a pilot who could barrel-roll under fire, but now she lived inside a body that flooded with adrenaline at any abrupt noise. Her granddaughter once touched her shoulder from behind and Elena spun and shoved her, nearly knocked her over. She had not meant to. She apologized for hours, but the shame stayed. She started to believe that she was no longer safe to be around, that her own reactions had turned her into a danger to the people she loved.

Last month, during a routine check-up, her doctor noticed her blood pressure was dangerously high. Elena admitted she was not sleeping, not eating well, that she had lost twelve pounds. The doctor asked if she had considered talking to someone. Elena said no. But that night, alone in her house, she realized she could not keep living inside this vigilance. She made an appointment with a psychologist. She is afraid that talking will make the pieces come faster, that she will have to smell the melons again or feel the concrete scrape her cheek. But she is also afraid of staying the same—of another year spent scanning rooms, avoiding jackets, and jumping at sirens. She does not know if she can be fixed. She only knows that she cannot keep going like this.
